title: Eliot Higgins: How Bellingcat Hunts Down the Truth | Podcast | In Good Company
description:
This live recorded episode of In Good Company features Eliot Higgins, founder of Bellingcat, the world's leading open source investigative collective — a self-taught college dropout who began tracking the Syrian war from his kitchen table. Together with Nicolai Tangen, he unpacks how his team unmasked Navalny's poisoners and tracked the downing of flight MH17 using nothing but publicly available data. Eliot explains the discipline at the heart of his work: never prejudge a situation, follow the evidence before forming an opinion, and guard against your own biases. The conversation also explores why speed matters when truth competes with lies, how AI gives people "permission to deny reality," and what disinformation means for democracy. Tune in for a fascinating conversation!

In Good Company is hosted by Nicolai Tangen, CEO of Norges Bank Investment Management. New episode out every Wednesday.

The podcast In Good Company is part of Norges Bank Investment Management, a podcast about our investments. We are transparent about how the fund is invested. In this podcast, you get a deeper insight into the companies the fund is invested in.

Our CEO, Nicolai Tangen, has in-depth interviews with the leaders of some of the largest companies in the world. You will get insight into their leadership principles, the company’s strategy and how they are dealing with a large investor like us. You will also learn more about our role as an owner of the companies.

You can read more about the podcast on https://www.nbim.no/en/publications/podcast/
summary: The episode features Nicolai Tangen, CEO of the Norwegian Sovereign Wealth Fund, hosting Eliot Higgins, founder of Bellingcat, to discuss open-source investigative methods that utilize publicly available data such as social media posts, satellite imagery, and flight tracking to uncover war crimes and conflicts. Higgins explains that his organization evolved from a volunteer-driven effort to win internet arguments into a structured entity with professional teams and a global community of researchers who prioritize evidence-based conclusions over preconceived opinions.

transcript: Hi everyone. I'm Nicolai Tangen, the CEO of the Norwegian Sovereign Wealth Fund. And today we have a very special episode. We are recording in front of a live audience of nearly 200 people. These are my colleagues at the Sovereign Wealth Fund. And we are joined by the very impressive Eliot Higgins, the founder of Bellingcat, the world's leading open-source investigative collective. Now, Eliot is not a spy, not a trained journalist, is actually a college dropout who taught himself to investigate war crimes from his kitchen table in Leicester. He's unmasked Russian assassins, exposed chemical weapons used in Syria, helped identify Navalny's poisoner. And I've been really looking forward to this, Eliot. Warm welcome. >> Thanks for having me on. >> So, just to start, what is Bellingcat? >> So, um Bellingcat does something called open-source investigations. So, that's using publicly available material to investigate a range of different topics. And really over the last 15 years, what is publicly available material has just mushroomed to just a huge extent. It's stuff like social media posts, uh satellite imagery available through things like Google Maps or other services, um all kinds of things like marine traffic data or air flight data that's also publicly available. So, we take all that data and then we investigate different things. And that's included uh chemical weapons attacks in Syria, the downing of Malaysian Airlines flight MH17, uh more recently a lot to do with America's bombing of Iran, uh ISIS and VHS raids in the US as well. So, >> How do you decide what to what to focus in on? >> Well, early on it's I mean, the whole field of open-source investigation was very much led by um kind of obsessive nerds on the internet just doing what was interesting to them. And really the big events were initially the Arab Spring in Syria, then the shooting down of MH17, then Russia's invasion of Ukraine. Um and so really that's kind of was just a bunch of volunteers doing things that were interesting to to them, but now we have teams who work on financial investigations, uh, what we call online ideologies, which is quite broad, uh, and conflict. >> So, how many how many different hotspots are you looking at at each point in time? >> Um, it it varies, but it's it's like at the moment we're looking at, uh, of course, what's happening in Iran, but we're also looking at, uh, the DRC and Sudan and other places where there's ongoing conflicts. Sometimes an investigation is a really, you know, multi-month month process. Sometimes it's reacting really quickly to events that are happening on the ground in different contexts. >> Now, you live here in Leicester. Uh, you got an organization in Holland, but you have a big network. Just how does it work? >> So, um, we have the central Bellingcat organization, which has about 35 staff members, mostly researchers and trainers. We then have a community of volunteers who we train and, uh, we can direct. That's about 200 people. There's also a Discord server where we have lots of people. It's kind of our community server that has about 43,000 people on it, and they, um, what's great about that is they kind of really have the values of Bellingcat, that it's really really about the research first before they form an opinion about something, and that's something that's quite quite rare in online spaces. But also, they find stuff that we're not looking at, and then that becomes kind of part of our process as well. >> are the values what would make me become one of your uh, kind of, what should we say, reporters or helpers or investigators? >> It's you never prejudge a situation. Just because you feel something should be the truth doesn't mean it actually is the truth. So, um, I I think that's a very important over contentious issues as well, where there tends to be two sides who just want to pick fights with each other on the internet. We're not interested in that. We want to look at the evidence first and draw our conclusions based off that evidence. Um, but also it's about inclusion as well. It's saying it's not just about what we do at Bellingcat, but teaching other people these skills so they can do their own investigations and form their own communities. So, community building with those values is something that's really a core part of what we do at Bellingcat. >> Now, we have just so much to learn from the methodology here. So, let's just always think, you know, what how can we how can we use this? But, let's just start with the beginning. 2012, you're sitting at your kitchen table and you're looking at YouTube clips from the Syrian war. What did you What did you see? >> Yeah, so um, I would really like to say I had a kind of noble >> why were you looking at YouTube clips from the Syrian war? >> I I wish I could say I had this noble intention to become a great human rights or journalist or something. No, I was arguing with people on the internet. And I wanted to win the arguments. And there were all these videos coming from places like Libya and Syria. And really in those kind of online communities, they were just being used as sticks to beat each other over the head with. They weren't fact-checking them. They were just saying, "Oh, this proves that I'm right and you're wrong." But, I just wanted to know what was going on in these places. So, I realized you could use satellite imagery to figure out where stuff was filmed. And we call this geolocation. It's a core skill now. But, at point it was just me winning arguments on the internet. But, I just really thought, "Well, this is kind of deepening my understanding of what's actually happening in these conflicts." And I started like posting about on Twitter and then doing a blog so I had more places to write with no intention of anyone ever taking me that seriously, but eventually they did. >> But, what did you see? So, I saw pictures. >> In Syria, I I didn't speak any Arabic so I was really looking at the content of the videos. And a lot of it showed unexploded munitions, um, eventually the aftermath of chemical weapon attacks. And I systematically tracked all the videos coming out of Syria because they basically used YouTube as their main distribution platform. Um, and those channels are usually run by like media centers or armed groups. So, you could actually have a catalog of all these channels and check them every single day. And no one else had figured out you could do that. So, every day I would just go through hundreds of videos from Syria looking for stuff that was new or unusual, really focusing on IDing weapons in particular. >> Then you started Bellingcat and that the Malaysian airline was shot down. Just how how did that case develop? >> So, um I was blogging um on a really awful looking blogspot website. I thought I needed more professional website and a better name. So, I launched Bellingcat in July 2014 and 3 days later MH17 was shot down. So, you have this kind of real mass movement on social media of people digging through stuff trying to figure things out. And Bellingcat kind of been became the kind of center point of a lot of that. So, I was publishing articles and then slowly building up a small team of kind of volunteer researchers who every day were digging through every bit of information about MH17 and searching for stuff. And that led us to finding all kinds of stuff that no one else anywhere had found like the origin of the missile launcher, where it had launched from, and other details like that. >> So, in the book they go into the story in great detail and you're going to see how that how that building that case. Now, the Russian Ministry of Defense weren't particularly pleased with you. >> Yeah, so we've had kind of an escalating campaign against us coming from Russia, really starting in 2015 with places like Russia Today and Sputnik News writing critical articles of us. That led to them trying to hack our emails, our website. Most recently there's been six Bulgarians who were jailed because they were spying on one of my colleagues for 2 years. And that was linked to the Russian FSB. So, there's really been an escalation of the years of how they've responded to our work. >> Now, we continued poisoning in the UK. What was that? >> Yeah, so um when the Skripal poisoning happened, we we couldn't really do much kind of in the initial moment. But when the identities of the poisoners was were released, they uh there was a Russian news site that got the flight manifest of the flight and their passport numbers were just a few digits apart, which is very suspicious. So, one of my former colleagues, Christo Grozev, he he's very good at using the kind of um what you call the kind of gray market of data in Russia. In Russia, basically all government data is for sale if you know the right people to speak to. >> Yeah. >> So, we got their passport registration. >> only in Russia or is that everywhere? >> It's mainly in Russia in our experience. There might be other places, but Russia's particularly bad for that cuz you know, the snake rots from the head. You know, it it's everyone's corrupt. So, we were buying things like the registration forms of passports and discovering they had the Russian MOD's phone number stamped on these guys' passport forms and using government databases of house registrations and car registrations to kind of unpick their identity. And eventually, that allowed us to find the real identity of these suspects. And so, what happened? So, um Well, part of it is we were the first people to show that these two guys who had just been on Russia Today saying they were tourists visiting Salisbury Cathedral and you know, talking about the 123 m spire. As they were on TV, we were getting the data ring showing that they were Russian spies and we were able to publish straight away. And that had a huge impact. We had like nearly every UK newspaper had our work on their front page the following day. Um and that really kind of led us then to the poisoning of Alexi Navalny as well because we discovered the network of chemical weapon scientists who were producing these chemical weapons, where they worked, and we were able to buy their phone records from people in Russia and hit see them phoning up FSB agents just before they're going to poison him. So, we could track the FSB agents as well cuz the phone records aren't just who you've called, it's every single cell phone tower you connect to, which can then be mapped out. You can actually follow people as they're moving around Europe and Russia, you know, minute by minute. And that's what we did with their data cuz Russia's so hideously corrupt in that way. And then he called them up. Yeah, he called them up. So, um we we had this um filmmaker with us who was just filming interesting things uh we were doing. And uh we thought wouldn't it be fun to call these people up now we've got their phone numbers. And [laughter] we thought it would be like over in 10 minutes. They'd all hang up or you know swear at us or something. And that happened for the first three or four calls. But then And then Navalny was the guy calling them up. So, then we tried we um spoofed the phone number of the FSB, called one of the guys up, and Navalny pretended to be uh kind of a an officer assessing the assassination attempt. It's worth tracking down the video and watching the whole thing. It's in the documentary we did, but the full video is an hour long. And he um got the guy to give him a blow-by-blow account of exactly how the poison had done. They'd basically got to his hotel room. You put poison on the seam of his underpants. And then when he put them on and went to the airport, it activated and uh started to nearly kill him. But he just gave us a blow-by-blow description then how he when they recovered Navalny and he was injured, they got his clothes and then cleaned his kind of underpants really carefully to get rid of the um poison they'd used in the assassination. And we recorded the whole thing and then that became our documentary. But we'd actually um Putin on the Friday after we did that phone call that just given a big speech about, you know, I've nothing to do with this. Navalny, you know, this is all untrue. And then on the Monday we were able to reveal this hour-long video of one of his spies explaining exactly how he did the poisoning. >> Do you check your underpants every day? >> [laughter] >> It's I mean I would advise everyone does that every day. >> I mean you're a you're a high-value target, right? >> Well, I mean it's it's something we have to take seriously. So, it's like at the moment I have West Midlands or East Midlands counter-terrorism police uh paying me the occasional visit to let me know what's going on in their world, which is always a bit disconcerting. Um you do have to be kind of a lot more security-aware, and aware of when something weird happens is you kind of think about is that just general weirdness, or is that a weirdness that's particularly focused on on me? It's like we had one guy after a big event we did in the Netherlands, a couple of the team were walking around, and this guy was following them around taking photos of them. So, they managed to snap a photo of him, thinking this guy's dodgy, maybe a spy. And they they spent weeks trying to figure out who this guy was. He was just a fan. He was just too shy to come up and say hello, so he was just taking photos from a distance, which is, yeah. We we contacted him and said, "Hey, by the way, please probably best not to do that in the future." >> Yeah, well, the the the people taking photos today are fans, too, so Um now, um we put I think we probably put in a jingle here because we're suddenly changing topics. The difference between now and 2012 in terms of what's available online in terms of material, what um what's the magnitude of change? >> Well, I I think one real change is the access we now have to satellite imagery. So, back in 2012, you were very reliant on things like Google Earth and Google Maps. Um now, for a monthly fee, we use Planet Labs, where we can only get daily imagery of of various sites, but we can actually task satellites to specific locations. So, sort of a James Bond, but if there's this area we're interested in, we can put in a tasking request and get satellite imagery of that in the next few days. Which, for our kind of work, when you're trying to verify stuff as quickly as possible, is incredibly useful. Each kind of conflict or situation has a kind of different a kind of um uh characteristics around how social media is used. So, with Syria, you know, Twitter, Facebook, and YouTube were where most stuff was being posted. With the conflict in Ukraine, especially since 2022, Telegram was the kind of big website. It constantly changes. If you're looking into criminal activity, you might find a lot on TikTok, for example. There's lots of people who do crimes and post them on TikTok, and then um do that for months and months and months until someone like us comes across it and unpicks the whole thing. So, um yeah, it's more you constantly have to learn, you have to see how different situations evolve, how technology is being used, and look for opportunities. And you know, there are like with Iran, the internet was shut down there for a very long time in the early parts of the current conflict. Um and that meant we had to use other techniques to analyze satellite data, for example, cuz there was no satellite data, either. So, we used a system that uses um infrareds um satellite imagery and compares the differences to them using a very complex program I can't possibly explain. But um that allows us to see a kind of heat map of where damage is occurring across Iran and elsewhere in the Middle East at a time when there was no visual satellite imagery of that kind of stuff. >> Supposedly, Israel hacked into normal civilian's camera all over Iran, right? To check out where the the leaders were. Do you hack into systems like that, too? >> No, and we we try to avoid crimes whenever possible. But [laughter] >> What what does that mean, try to avoid? >> Well, well, it's For example, the um sometimes I mean, pretty much everything we do is a criminal offense in Russia at the moment, mainly cuz we did it and then they made it a criminal offense to do it. So, for example, the um Russian soldiers used to post loads of social on social media about where they were, what they were up to, their friends. And we used that to reconstruct exactly where they were on the MH17. But then the Russian um government passed a law to ban soldiers from doing that ever again, partly cuz of what we were doing in terms of that. But it's also like the stuff we're doing with the um Navalny and Skripal investigations. We wouldn't buy data anymore, because that's become that's kind of of area we felt even when we were doing it, but it's kind of a choice of, you know, we we knew how the data was and if we ignored it then people were literally being killed with chemical weapons and we found that there were multiple people who were killed like that that hadn't even really made it to the media. So, there was that kind of complex ethical conversation we had around that. >> What's the weirdest source of data you've used ever? >> Um This wasn't one of our investigations, but it always I think it definitely ticks the weird box. So, a a couple years ago there was a Instagram post that was being shared on social media. It had been copied and pasted and it was supposedly from Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez's social media account and it showed a pair of women's legs in the bath. It's like a saucy photo. Now, very quickly the WikiFeet community, which is the foot fetish community, who rates people's feet, immediately said, "That's not her feet. We know what her feet look like. It's actually this person's feet." And they found the original photograph of it. So, but you know, in all of this work, I mean, if you go back to um you know, the rendition flights that were happening in the early 2000s, it was plane spotters who found that network. So, people with really really specific interests and hobbies can actually be a really useful source of information. You just have to kind of know what kind of people out there and how to interact with them safely, I guess. >> So, nerds nerds are good. >> Nerds and perverts, yes. >> [laughter] >> We have the old nerd, too. We love them. >> [laughter] >> What's the most shocking piece of disinformation that you've seen ever? >> Oh god, I mean, it's so so constant. It's like there's an ongoing campaign from Russia at the moment. It's called various things. One of them is the Russian doll campaign cuz what they've been doing is making fake videos of news sites, including myself. And they made a 3D animated kind of PlayStation 2 era graphics avatar of me to do some of the videos. Uh, another thing they did in that campaign. So, a typical video would be like, you know, the Armenian president is a drug addict. Not that anyone would even bother interacting with that post, but they just churned dozens of these out every single week. And they sent email them to us directly, so we engage with them, which we don't. But, they included jigsaw pieces in some of these posts. So, it'd be the fake news video and a jigsaw piece. And, um, they were all numbered. So, I started piecing them together over a period of weeks and weeks. And what it was, it was a jigsaw puzzle of my face on a pile of poo with, um, "Belling at Elliot Higgins" as the logo. Sorry my language, but they'd included this in their disinformation as a kind of weird personalized message to me. But, things I like doing jigsaws, so for me this is just fun. And then I had like something I could kind of post on social media as well. So, it was like, "This is just keep doing it." They actually started a third jigsaw puzzle. There were two, and they did a third one. And I think I had posted so much about the second one they did, they actually got told to stop doing it, which I was very disappointed about cuz it looked good. >> What are we up against in terms of number of people? What are What kind of the resources, let's say, uh, in Russia to conduct those kind of campaigns? What are we What are we What are we What are we up against here? >> Well, I mean, it's kind of a what we're looking at is a kind of development of the Internet Research Agency, which really kind of dominated the kind of 2016 scene. Um, that was linked to people who had now been killed by the Russian government. So, now it's being run by another oligarch. But, they're they're dealing with hundreds of people who are doing this. The The thing with disinformation, though, we tend to treat it as a kind of foreign actor issue, but a lot of disinformation and misinformation comes from online communities who generally believe they're creating good, useful information, but also have kind of grifters in that community and sometimes Russian or you know, foreign interference that's kind of amplifying those communities. But for disinformation to work, you need people who want to engage with it. And this is why a lot of this recent Russian disinformation doesn't work. They did a huge campaign around Armenia, hundreds of videos, fakes, all sorts. It got no engagement because not really that many people who speak English on social media really care about what's happening in Armenian politics. So it got no genuine uplift. >> When you start these uh investigations, how do you make sure do you have like a hypothesis and you test it, or how do you how do you work? How do you make sure that you aren't biased in your research? >> Yeah, I mean, it depends on the starting point and the scale of something. So, um with the Alex Wrecker and Manny Good Shootings in Minnesota, there straight away you had videos that were being shared and dissected on social media. So, in that case, what we were trying to do is get information out quickly that looked at certain key claims, which we could say yes, this is true or not. So, Alex Wrecker was disarmed and then shot, and that became a point of contention, but we released a video that kind of synchronized multiple videos to show the moment he was disarmed and then shot in one complete sequence rather than the fragments that were out there. So, that's when you kind of have to respond quickly because there is a discourse, and you know, the government's going to lie about it, too. But in other cases, it could be a lot more, you know, gather a huge amount of information, start looking at what patterns it's showing you, um try to verify as much of that information as possible. So, uh we're looking at kind of Israelis um air air strikes in Lebanon very, very recently, and that was a huge data set we were looking at rather than kind of individual videos and focusing on just one particular incident. So, there's just it's a matter of scale and you know, what question we're trying to answer. >> You mentioned the importance of speed in the Minnesota case. Just why is speed so important? Why is it so important to to the truth out before uh false perceptions have uh kind of established themselves. >> Cuz generally once people feel they know the truth about a subject, they'll not change their mind about it. And in those moments when there's, you know, just a few hours where there's a really uh vigorous discourse online, and you know that it's going to be a government that's going to come out with a version of events that's probably not going to match reality, trying to get as much information into that discourse is important because people take those kind of objects you create and then spread them across multiple websites where all this discourse is occurring. So, you don't have to distribute it just as as like a single node. You're kind of can rely on other people to pick that up and take it elsewhere. When it's something that's uh kind of longer-term, kind of deeper investigation, you don't have that kind of engagement happening. So, you have to really approach that in a different way, both in how you investigate it, but also then how you distribute that information. How do you reach the audiences you want to see it? >> So, how fast do you need to be now? Let's say there is a shooting, which is bad. Where How fast How quickly do you need to be out there with a narrative? >> Well, I mean, I I I think you've got at best two or three hours in many cases, if it's something like those um shootings in Minnesota. Um something that took a little bit longer, but was still kind of influenced the discourse, which if we look at the um Iranian um school bombing where the girls were killed, um we found a video of Tomahawk missiles hit striking close to that building, but not on it. But we got that information out there um probably within about 48 hours of the air strikes happening. And then Donald Trump was being asked about, you know, why is there a video of Tomahawk missiles? By journalists who had seen our work, know where reliable, and then could actually ask that question knowing that, you know, that is a fact, not just something that they've kind of read on the internet and rumored. And then Donald Trump responded by saying, "Well, the Iranians have Tomahawk missiles as well." Which is completely ridiculous, but he was forced into that position because we could present verifiable evidence. How much more are governments lying now compared to 10 years ago? I mean, it depends on the government, I think, more than >> didn't want to be I didn't want to be specific. >> Certain governments that are kind of to the west of this country, they are lying The thing is it's kind of a it's authoritarian capture ultimately, because then it becomes about loyalty tests. It doesn't come about the truth, it becomes about how you demonstrate your loyalty to the the in-group, and then how you can define the out-group by their refusal to tow the line. So, this is really what we're saying seeing in the US is authoritarian capture of various institutions, the presidency, the kind of bending of the knee of various organizations, where the truth is no longer important. It's all about those loyalty tests. >> How do you think this will develop? >> Uh so, a lot of my work at the moment looks at issues around disinformation and democratic theory and kind of where we've got how we've got to where we are at the moment. I think the the the one thing that really worries me about that work, and I've spent a long time doing this, is that the way we've kind of set up our society and information system now has changed completely. We've gone from this information system that was top-down, elite-controlled, uh and also normalized because of that. We had institutions, the media, who, you know, they kind of controlled the flow of information to the public to a large extent. And the public were recipients of information. And in that relationship, the public had to trust those institutions to produce verifiable information that they could be deliberated on it procedurally through courts, through parliaments, and then people would be held to account for wrongdoing. And that was the public the kind of social contract we had with those institutions. That's now collapsed into a peer-to-peer, many-to-many information system, where institutions are competing for attention with the public in systems that rewards engagement over the truth. And those platforms like X, for example, that monetize their social media process, rewards basically engagement more than anything. So, what that leads to is a system where populist, authoritarian, and conspiratorial ideas perform really well because they don't need the procedural certainty behind it. You just say this is true, and people nod their head because they're prepared to believe that in a way. >> And the whole clickbait >> Yeah, yeah, it's just all about, you know, what engages people rather than what's truthful. And we see this often around conflicts where there's a lot of public engagement. You know, the situation in Gaza produced a lot of fake information because people just wanted to get the clicks and monetize the engagement that they were get getting on platforms like X. >> One of the bigger questions on on democracy, [clears throat] I mean, you talk about verification, deliberation, accountability. Could you just explain briefly the concept? >> Yeah, so you can understand democracy as having three core functions when it works well. That's verification, how do we know what's true? Deliberation, how do we decide to what we do on that? And then accountability is how we hold powerful the powerful to account. And when that functions, it restrains power. But what we tend to see more in our democracies is a kind of performative version of that where it's not really about holding the powerful to account or real verification, it's about getting elected. It's about building a coalition of voters who'll be enough to get you in. But that then slides into a form of simulated democracy which becomes disordered where verification is now about a predecided set of truths. And if you go outside of that, you become attacked by the in-group. Deliberation is also about really identifying who's loyal rather than identifying what to do on this information. And accountability is always targeted outwards from the in-group. And you can look over to the US and see that happening very, very clearly every single day. >> And so what can democracies do to counteract this? Well, unfortunately it's a big issue and it requires a lot of involvement with lots of different sectors. I I speak to policy makers, government, people working in civil society about these issues and there's a recognition there's a huge problem. >> Yeah. >> The problem we've got is really since 2016 has been defined as an issue of foreign interference, of disinformation. And that if somehow we can get rid of that issue that false information, society will fix itself and democracy will flourish again. Problem is that's complete nonsense. It treats disinformation and the problems it causes as a kind of supply side issue. That if only we get rid of the supply then all these problems will fix itself. But really that's driven when people feel a sense of betrayal, of distrust in those institutions and they look for alternative sources in these online spaces where engagement is rewarded over accuracy. So even though they might be trying to seek this truth, they're going into environments which are not designed for truth seeking. They're designed for engagement. So people get drawn towards more conspiratorial ways of thinking and again authoritarianism, populism and conspiracy theories perform extremely well and slow procedural verification through institutions, the media, through Bellingcat doesn't perform as well in those environments. >> Do you think any of this is important for us as a long-term investor? >> Well, I think when reality becomes contest, I mean Does anyone work on anything to do with Iran at the moment and do you know what the hell's going on? Cuz day-to-day the story of what's happening changes. So So without that reliability without being able to rely on what could be truthful and what's not, then it's very hard to make any real, you know, tactical strategic decisions about things. And this is where open source investigation is so valuable. I mean we train people in all kinds of different sectors. I mean we've trained investment firms, journalists, you know, all kinds of people to do this kind of work. >> But if you take if you take the Iran conflict as an example, how much information flow is there now from each side? I mean, how would you think they compare? >> Um >> [sighs] >> information I mean >> Cuz we got so little information >> is also information. It's just very poor quality information that you can't trust. So, you then have to use other ways of figuring out what's going on. And this is why a balance account we've been looking at Iran, there is a limit on satellite imagery and social media information that has been useful in the past, but there are other ways to look at what's going on there. >> How is AI changing all of this? >> Um I think AI gives people a permission structure to deny reality. So, if they see a picture they don't like or a video, they can just say, "Well, that's AI." And that's the kind of end of their engagement with that particular object.
